Solution 1's answer of 21 is the most plausible. I could only check that this is a lower bound, not that it is the maximum.

**Solution 1.** Its guess is not justified, but it points at a real model. Take the flag variety \(B_3/P_{1,2}\) (isotropic point–line flags in a 7-dimensional quadratic space). This has dimension 8, and the symmetry algebra \(\mathfrak{so}(7)\) has dimension 21.

I checked the growth of the natural distribution on it by counting root spaces, with the Levi factor \(A_1\) generated by \(\alpha_3\):
- The rank-1 part from \(\alpha_1\) and the rank-2 part from \(\alpha_2,\ \alpha_2+\alpha_3\) give a rank-3 distribution.
- Brackets then add \(\alpha_1+\alpha_2\) and \(\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3\), which gives 2 dimensions.
- They also add \(2\alpha_2+\alpha_3\), which gives 1 dimension.
- So \(D^2\) has rank \(3+2+1=6\).
- The remaining two root spaces, \(\alpha_1+2\alpha_2+\alpha_3\) and \(\alpha_1+2\alpha_2+2\alpha_3\), give growth \((3,6,8)\).

So a distribution with the required growth has a 21-dimensional symmetry algebra, and the maximum is at least 21.

**Solution 3.** Its value 15 is below this lower bound, so it cannot be the maximum. Its argument also only bounds the grading-preserving part of the prolongation, not the full algebra.

**Solution 2.** Its claim of infinite dimension is not credible. The vector fields \(a(y_{12},y_{13})\partial_{y_{12}}+\dots\) do not commute with the left-invariant generators in general, because those generators depend on the other coordinates. The finite-type theory for bracket-generating distributions of this kind also argues against an infinite symmetry algebra.

CHOICE: 1
